title: Problems: false fits, wrong multiples, power and screens of pairs

items.prose: Two paper mills' share prices are simulated. $x_t$ is a random walk with daily shocks of sd £0.40, and $y_t = 3 + 0.75x_t + u_t$. Here $u_t$ is stationary and independent of $x$, with a long-run sd of £0.50. A trader uses the multiple 0.6 instead of 0.75, so his gap is $y_t - 0.6x_t - 3 = 0.15x_t + u_t$.

parts.question: How much variance does the walk part $0.15x_t$ gain each day, in pounds squared? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: One day's shock to $x$ has variance $0.40^2 = 0.16$, and the multiple scales it by $0.15^2$: $0.0225 \times 0.16 = 0.0036$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Square the 0.15 and square the £0.40, then multiply.

byKey.sd-not-squared: You used the shock sd, 0.40, where its square belongs. A variance needs $0.40^2 = 0.16$.
byKey.multiple-not-squared: You multiplied by 0.15 instead of $0.15^2$. Scaling a series by $c$ scales its variance by $c^2$.
byKey.neither-squared: That is the sd of one day's move in $0.15x_t$, £0.06. Square it for the variance.

explain.text: The walk part moves by 0.15 times each shock, so one day's move has an sd of $0.15 \times 0.40 = £0.06$. Its square, 0.0036, is the variance each day adds. The true gap gains nothing: it stays at $u_t$.

parts.question: Using 0.0036 a day from part 1, and $u$'s variance of $0.50^2 = 0.25$, what is the sd of the trader's gap on day 500? Count from day 0, when $x$ is known, and give your answer in pounds to 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The walk part has variance $0.15^2 \times 0.40^2 \times 500 = 1.8$ and $u$ adds 0.25, so the sd is $\sqrt{2.05} = £1.43$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the variance $0.15x_t$ has gathered since day 0 to the variance of $u_t$, then take the root.

byKey.no-u: That is the walk part alone, $\sqrt{1.8}$. The gap still holds $u_t$, which adds its variance of 0.25.
byKey.variance: That is the variance, 2.05. The sd is its root.
byKey.sd-not-squared: You used the shock sd, 0.40, where its square belongs. Each day adds $0.15^2 \times 0.40^2 = 0.0036$.
byKey.multiple-not-squared: You multiplied by 0.15 instead of $0.15^2$. Scaling a series by $c$ scales its variance by $c^2$.

explain.text: From day 0, $0.15x_t$ gathers 500 shocks of variance $0.15^2 \times 0.16 = 0.0036$ each, 1.8 in all. As $u$ is independent of $x$, the variances add to 2.05, whose root is £1.43.

parts.question: The walk part's variance is $0.0036t$ and $u$'s is 0.25. On what day does the trader's gap first have an sd above twice £0.50? Give a whole number of days.

feedback.correct: Twice £0.50 is £1.00, a variance of 1. So $0.0036t + 0.25 > 1$ needs $t > 208.3$: day 209.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Twice the sd is four times the variance, so solve $0.0036t + 0.25 > 4 \times 0.25$.

byKey.no-subtract: You set the walk part alone equal to 1. The gap already has 0.25 from $u$, so the walk must add only 0.75.
byKey.doubled-variance: You doubled the variance, which needs only $0.0036t + 0.25 > 0.5$. Twice the sd is four times the variance: 1.
byKey.round-down: On day 208 the variance is $0.7488 + 0.25 = 0.9988$, still below 1. Day 209 is the first above it.

explain.text: Doubling the sd means four times the variance: $4 \times 0.25 = 1$. The walk part must supply 0.75, which takes $0.75/0.0036 = 208.3$ days, so day 209 is the first.

parts.question: On 1,600 days, Engle-Granger's step one regresses $y$ on $x$. Which statement is right?

options.text: Least squares lands near 0.75, because any other multiple leaves a growing walk in the gap; $y - 0.6x - 3$ is I(1)
Least squares lands near 0.6, because $y - 0.6x - 3$ still contains the stationary $u$
options.why: Holding $u$ is not enough. The leftover $0.15x$ is a walk, so its variance grows and least squares moves away from 0.6.

options.text: $y - 0.6x - 3$ is stationary, only with a wider band than the true gap's
options.why: No fixed band holds that gap. Its variance grows by 0.0036 a day without limit.

options.text: No multiple can work, because $x$ and $y$ are each I(1)
options.why: Two I(1) series can still have a stationary combination. Here $y - 0.75x - 3$ is exactly $u$.

feedback.correct: Correct. A wrong multiple leaves a walk whose variance grows without limit, so least squares settles near the true 0.75.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what happens to the variance of $0.15x_t$ as $t$ grows.

byKey.near-trader: Holding $u$ is not enough. The leftover $0.15x$ is a walk, so its variance grows and least squares moves away from 0.6.
byKey.wide-band: No fixed band holds that gap. Its variance grows by 0.0036 a day without limit.
byKey.none: Two I(1) series can still have a stationary combination. Here $y - 0.75x - 3$ is exactly $u$.

explain.text: On day 1,600 the trader's gap has variance $0.0036 \times 1{,}600 + 0.25 = 6.01$, against 0.25 for the true gap. Least squares picks the multiple with the smallest sum of squared gaps, so it is pulled to 0.75. Its residual is then close to $u$, and step two rejects a unit root.

items.prose: A strategist regresses the daily level of cocoa futures on the level of a semiconductor index. She has 750 days, and the two levels have correlation $r = -0.45$. For the slope, use $|t| = |r|\sqrt{(n - 2)/(1 - r^2)}$.

parts.question: What is $|t|$ for her levels regression? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $n - 2 = 748$ over $1 - r^2$, take the root, then multiply by $|r|$.

byKey.no-root: You left out the square root. $\sqrt{937.9} = 30.63$, and $0.45 \times 30.63 = 13.78$.
byKey.r-squared: You multiplied by $r^2 = 0.2025$. The formula multiplies by $|r| = 0.45$.
byKey.one-minus-r: You divided by $1 - |r| = 0.55$. The formula has $1 - r^2 = 0.7975$.

explain.text: With $n - 2 = 748$ and $1 - r^2 = 0.7975$, $|t| = 0.45 \times 30.63 = 13.78$. The textbook's rule asks only for 1.96, so this fit clears it seven times over.

parts.question: At 750 days, what is the smallest $|r|$ that already gives $|t| > 1.96$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Set $|t| = 1.96$, square both sides and solve for $r^2$.

explain.text: Set $|t| = 1.96$ and solve: $r^2 = 1.96^2/(748 + 1.96^2) = 0.00511$, so $|r| = 0.0715$. Any correlation past that passes the 5% rule on 750 days. Two wandering levels clear it with ease.

parts.question: She extends the sample to 1,500 days and the correlation stays at −0.45. Part 1 gave $|t| = 13.78$ on 750 days. What is $|t|$ now? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Keep $r = -0.45$ and use $n - 2 = 1{,}498$ in the formula.

byKey.doubled: $|t|$ does not double with the days. It grows like $\sqrt{n - 2}$, so it rises by about 1.41 times.
byKey.unchanged: The correlation is the same, but $n$ is not. $|t|$ rises with $\sqrt{n - 2}$.

explain.text: With $r$ fixed, $|t|$ grows like $\sqrt{n - 2}$. Doubling the days multiplies it by about 1.41, from 13.78 to 19.50. Nothing about the two markets has changed.

parts.question: Her Engle-Granger test on the 1,500 days gives a residual statistic of −2.41. Which conclusion is right?

options.text: No evidence of a tie: −2.41 is above even the 10% value, about −3.04, so the levels $t$ cannot be read
A tie: a $t$ of 19.50 is far beyond 1.96
options.why: Between two I(1) levels that $t$ grows with the sample whatever the link, so it carries no evidence.

options.text: A tie at 10%: −2.41 is negative and close to the ADF value −2.86
options.why: A residual is judged against MacKinnon's values, about −3.04 at 10%, and −2.41 is not below even −2.86.

options.text: No tie in levels, but the $t$ of 19.50 proves a link between daily moves
options.why: A levels $t$ says nothing about daily moves. To ask about those, regress the changes.

feedback.correct: Correct. Until a residual rejects, the levels $t$ cannot be read, and here it mostly measures the sample length.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare −2.41 with MacKinnon's residual values, then ask what that means for the levels $t$.

byKey.t-proves: Between two I(1) levels that $t$ grows with the sample whatever the link, so it carries no evidence.
byKey.near-adf: A residual is judged against MacKinnon's values, about −3.04 at 10%, and −2.41 is not below even −2.86.
byKey.daily-link: A levels $t$ says nothing about daily moves. To ask about those, regress the changes.

explain.text: −2.41 lies above −3.04, −3.34 and −3.90, so Engle-Granger finds no evidence of a tie at any usual level. Until a residual rejects, the levels regression has to be treated as spurious, as in lesson 1. Its $t$ grew from 13.78 to 19.50 only because the sample doubled.

items.prose: A desk plans how many days of history it needs to test two cable makers' shares as a pair. It expects their gap to behave like an AR(1), $u_t = 0.96u_{t-1} + \eta_t$. Engle-Granger's step two fits $\Delta\hat u_t = \gamma\hat u_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$. As a rough guide, $t_\gamma$ is about $\gamma$ divided by $\sqrt{(1 - \phi^2)/n}$, the slope's standard error on $n$ days.

parts.question: What value of $\gamma$ does this gap imply? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Taking $u_{t-1}$ from both sides gives $\Delta u_t = (0.96 - 1)u_{t-1} + \eta_t$, so $\gamma = -0.04$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Take $u_{t-1}$ from both sides of the AR(1).

byKey.phi: That is $\phi$, the slope of $u_t$ on $u_{t-1}$. Step two regresses the change, so its slope is $\phi - 1$.
byKey.sign: A gap that reverts tends to fall when it is high, so $\gamma = \phi - 1$ is negative.

explain.text: Step two regresses the day's change on yesterday's level. Writing $\Delta u_t = u_t - u_{t-1}$ turns the AR(1) into $\Delta u_t = (\phi - 1)u_{t-1} + \eta_t$. So $\gamma = 0.96 - 1 = -0.04$.

parts.question: Using $\gamma = -0.04$, what $t_\gamma$ does the rough guide give on 250 days? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $1 - 0.96^2 = 0.0784$ and $n = 250$ into the standard error, then divide $\gamma$ by it.

byKey.one-minus-phi: You used $1 - \phi = 0.04$. The standard error has $1 - \phi^2 = 0.0784$.
byKey.no-root: You left out the square root. The standard error is $\sqrt{0.0784/250} = 0.0177$.
byKey.sign: $t_\gamma$ keeps the sign of $\gamma = -0.04$, so it is negative.

explain.text: $1 - 0.96^2 = 0.0784$, so the standard error is $\sqrt{0.0784/250} = 0.0177$. The guide gives $t_\gamma = -0.04/0.0177 = -2.26$. That is above even MacKinnon's 10% value, about −3.04, so a year of data would usually miss this tie.

parts.question: Using $t_\gamma = -0.04\sqrt{n/0.0784}$, on how many days does the guide's statistic first reach MacKinnon's 5% value, −3.34? Give a whole number of days.

feedback.correct: $0.04/0.28 = 0.1429$, so the statistic is $-0.1429\sqrt n$. It reaches −3.34 when $\sqrt n = 23.38$, so $n = 546.6$: 547 days.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Set $0.04\sqrt{n/0.0784} = 3.34$, square both sides and round up.

byKey.linear: You scaled the 250 days by $3.34/2.26$. The statistic grows like $\sqrt n$, so the days grow like its square.
byKey.adf: −2.86 is the ADF value for a raw series. A fitted residual is judged against MacKinnon's −3.34.
byKey.round-down: On 546 days the guide gives $-3.338$, just short of −3.34. Round up to 547.

explain.text: As $\sqrt{0.0784} = 0.28$, the guide's statistic is $-(0.04/0.28)\sqrt n = -0.1429\sqrt n$. It reaches −3.34 at $n = (3.34 \times 0.28/0.04)^2 = 546.6$. So the guide asks for 547 days, more than twice the 250.

parts.question: A second candidate's gap has $\phi = 0.98$. By the same guide, on how many days does its statistic first reach −3.34? Give a whole number of days.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Redo part 3 with $\gamma = 0.98 - 1$ and $1 - 0.98^2 = 0.0396$.

byKey.doubled: Halving $\gamma$ does not simply double the days: $1 - \phi^2$ also shrinks, from 0.0784 to 0.0396.
byKey.phi-unchanged: You kept $1 - \phi^2 = 0.0784$ from the first gap. With $\phi = 0.98$ it is 0.0396.
byKey.one-minus-phi: You used $1 - \phi = 0.02$ in the standard error. It has $1 - \phi^2 = 0.0396$.

explain.text: The slower gap has $\gamma = -0.02$ and $\sqrt{0.0396} = 0.1990$, so the guide's statistic is $-0.1005\sqrt n$. That reaches −3.34 at $n = 1{,}104.4$, over four years of daily closes. A slow tie tested on one year will usually fail, though it is real.

items.prose: A desk tests 1,200 pairs of mid-cap shares for cointegration, each by Engle-Granger at the 5% level on two years of daily closes. Suppose 36 of the pairs, 3%, are truly tied and the other 1,164 are not. On two years of data the test catches a true tie with chance 0.40.

parts.question: On average, how many of the 36 tied pairs pass the test? Give 1 decimal place.

feedback.correct: Each tied pair passes with chance 0.40, so $36 \times 0.40 = 14.4$ of them pass on average.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the number of tied pairs by the chance that the test catches one.

byKey.no-power: That counts every tied pair as found. On two years the test finds each one only with chance 0.40.
byKey.miss-rate: 21.6 is $36 \times 0.60$, the tied pairs the test misses. The passes are $36 \times 0.40$.
byKey.all-pairs: You applied 0.40 to all 1,200 pairs. Only the 36 tied ones pass at that rate.

explain.text: The test's power, 0.40, is its chance of catching a real tie. Of 36 tied pairs it finds 14.4 on average and misses the other 21.6.

parts.question: Using 14.4 from part 1, how many pairs pass in all, on average? Give 1 decimal place.

feedback.correct: The untied pairs add $1{,}164 \times 0.05 = 58.2$ false passes, so the desk expects $14.4 + 58.2 = 72.6$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the untied pairs that pass at the 5% level to the 14.4 tied ones.

byKey.all-untied: You took 5% of all 1,200 pairs. The 36 tied pairs are counted in the 14.4, so take 5% of 1,164.
byKey.false-only: 58.2 is the untied pairs that pass. Add the 14.4 tied ones as well.
byKey.no-power: 94.2 counts all 36 tied pairs as passing. Part 1 found only 14.4 of them.

explain.text: A 5% test passes an untied pair with chance 0.05, so 1,164 of them give 58.2 passes. With the 14.4 real ones, the desk expects 72.6 pairs on its list.

parts.question: Using 14.4 and 72.6, what share of the passes is truly tied? Give a percentage to 1 decimal place.

feedback.correct: $14.4/72.6 = 19.8\%$: about one pass in five is a real tie.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the tied pairs that pass by all the pairs that pass.

byKey.all-untied: 19.4% divides by 74.4, which takes 5% of all 1,200 pairs. The total is 72.6.
byKey.power: 40% is the chance of catching a tie, a share of the 36 tied pairs. This asks for a share of the 72.6 passes.
byKey.false-share: 80.2% is the share of the passes that are false. The real share is the rest, 19.8%.
byKey.over-false: You divided 14.4 by the 58.2 false passes. Divide by all 72.6 passes.

explain.text: Only 14.4 of the 72.6 passes are tied, 19.8%. The 5% level holds each untied pair's chance of passing at 0.05. But the 1,164 untied pairs outnumber the 36 tied ones about 32 to 1.

parts.question: On four years of closes the test catches a true tie with chance 0.85. The untied pairs still give 58.2 false passes. What share of the passes is truly tied now? Give a percentage to 1 decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the tied pairs that pass at 0.85, add the 58.2 false passes, then divide.

byKey.power: 85% is the share of tied pairs found. The question asks what share of all passes they make.
byKey.all-untied: 33.8% adds 5% of all 1,200 pairs, 60. The untied pairs give 58.2.
byKey.old-total: 42.1% divides by part 2's total, 72.6. The tied passes rose to 30.6, so the total is 88.8.
byKey.false-share: 65.5% is the false share. The tied share is $30.6/88.8 = 34.5\%$.

explain.text: A longer window more than doubles the tied pairs found, from 14.4 to 30.6. The false passes stay at 58.2, so the real share rises only to 34.5%.

parts.question: The desk also moves to the 1% level, where four years catch a true tie with chance 0.65. Part 4 gave 34.5% at the 5% level. What share of the passes is truly tied now? Give a percentage to 1 decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Redo both counts: 0.65 of the tied pairs and 1% of the untied ones.

byKey.old-power: 72.4% keeps the chance 0.85. A stricter level catches fewer ties: use 0.65.
byKey.five-percent: 28.7% still takes 5% of the untied pairs. At the 1% level they give $1{,}164 \times 0.01 = 11.64$.
byKey.false-share: 33.2% is the false share. The tied share is the rest, 66.8%.

explain.text: The stricter level gives up 7.2 real passes but removes 46.56 false ones. Two passes in three, 66.8%, are now real, against 19.8% at the start.
